items.title: The next customer brands need to win over isn’t human—and it doesn’t care how big your company is
items.summary:
Tati Lindenberg has a challenge on her hands. As global CMO of Unilever’s homecare division, she’s made her name by marketing to humans—often by playing on senses and emotions. But soon, she’ll need to market to a different kind of customer—one that doesn’t feel, sense, or care how big your company is. That is the AI agent. 

“The store, online or offline, has always been where the decision is made. The AI answer is becoming a new kind of shelf,” says Lindenberg. “In that world, a brand needs to be recognised, trusted and preferred by people and by machines.”

In the U.K., 52% of shoppers have used AI for at least one shopping task in the past three months, according to McKinsey research. In China—where adoption of AI is more advanced—that figure rises to 80%.

The power of agents in decision-making is growing. Currently, most consumers use AI to conduct research and will make the ultimate decision on what to buy themselves. But soon, a substantial number could trust agents to handle the entire process. 

Mastercard forecasts that one in 10 people will routinely use AI agents to shop and pay by 2030. Meta’s personal AI agent Muse, which is capable of researching products and making purchases, is expected to launch in the U.K. “within weeks.” 

Purchases of Unilever’s beauty, wellbeing, and home care products are more likely to be delegated to AI, according to Nick Carroll, Mintel’s retail principal strategist. “In general, consumers are most interested in automating those less emotive and most regularly purchased categories,” he says. Mintel data shows household products…
items.t: The next customer brands need to win over isn’t human—and it doesn’t care how big your company is

items.title: ‘Walkie-talkie and paper just doesn’t cut it anymore’: FAA ground stop exposes air travel tech Delta’s CEO likens to the 1960s
items.summary:
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration made the rare decision to halt all flight departures nationwide, throwing travel plans into chaos. More than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart from U.S. airports after the order took effect. The agency lifted the ground stop more than four hours later, but two days on, airlines were still struggling to get flights moving again.

FlightAware counted 9,201 canceled flights Friday , 6,698 Saturday and at least 1,956 by Sunday evening , roughly 17,850 cancellations over three days involving flights within, into or out of the U.S.

Restarting the system was the easy part. Getting aircraft, crews and schedules back in sync is harder, and much of that work still runs on radios, spreadsheets and manual communication, according to Javier Vidal, co-founder and CEO of Moonware, a company that develops software to coordinate airport ground operations.

“Many airlines operate flights where the plane goes to one city and then it goes to the next city and then it goes to the next city,” Vidal told Fortune . “So it’s not like there’s one big ground stop and then everything can resume normally… Those planes need to be repositioned to the right cities.”

What triggered Friday’s ground stop 

Only two other nationwide ground stops have been ordered this century: after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and during an FAA computer system failure in January 2023 .

This one was serious enough to trigger a response at the highest levels of government. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the White House Situation Room and the…
items.t: ‘Walkie-talkie and paper just doesn’t cut it anymore’: FAA ground stop exposes air travel tech Delta’s CEO likens to the 1960s

items.title: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often
items.summary:
For years, Gen Z has been cast as the generation that would rather ask ChatGPT than its own manager . New research points to a sharper divide, one that has less to do with age than with rank. The people leaning hardest on AI are the ones at the top.

Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, according to Charter’s AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job.

About a third of managers and executives say they trust AI more than their own judgment on work decisions, compared with 16.3% of non-managers. Executives are also more than twice as likely as workers to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague.

Gen Z, by contrast, approaches AI with some skepticism. In the Voices of Gen Z study from Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, and GSV Ventures, a survey of 1,572 Americans ages 14 to 29, 69% of employed Gen Zers say they trust work completed without AI more than AI-assisted work. Only 3% put the most faith in work produced entirely by AI.

That skepticism isn’t avoidance. The same survey found that 51% of Gen Zers use generative AI at least weekly. They just treat it as a supporting character, not the lead.

The AI trust gap tracks rank more than age 

Brian Elliott, Charter’s executive-in-residence, who co-led the AI Pulse research , says where someone sits at the table matters more than the year they were born. “We surveyed over 5,000 AI users at work and found sharper divides by career stage than by age,” he tells Fortune .

Part of it comes down to the job itself. “AI is great at…
items.t: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often

items.title: The resignation of Jensen Huang marks the end of an era. And not the one you think
items.summary:
Just days after the American electorate delivered a sweeping midterm rebuke that materially curtailed Donald Trump’s presidential power, the independent board of Nvidia— the world’s most valuable firm for much of the year—launched an investigation into its own CEO, Jensen Huang. 

The board’s focus was Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. His resignation swiftly followed. In less than a week, we witnessed the core machinery of accountability brought to bear on two of the most powerful men in the world. 

But while the midterm outcome is being heralded as a resounding revival of healthy democracy, the Nvidia example should not be mistaken for a corporate oversight renaissance. Instead, Nvidia’s boardroom intervention may mark the end of a governance era, especially when it comes to frontier AI firms. 

Nvidia has a single-class share structure, meaning the CEO—who has a minority of votes at under 4% —remains accountable to an independent board. Elsewhere however, the governance guardrails for other powerful tech executives are rapidly eroding—a dismantling revealed in IPO filings—just as these companies amass unprecedented global influence. 

SpaceX and Anthropic’s recent filings disclose that post IPO, their founders have a majority of shareholder votes via multi-class share structures , dual-class for SpaceX, and a novel five-class system for Anthropic. Popularized by Alphabet and Meta , this shields them from short-term market pressures, and the appeal is clear: in the U.S., a record 36% of new listings in the first half of 2026 had dual-class shares. Yet by…
items.t: The resignation of Jensen Huang marks the end of an era. And not the one you think

items.title: Priced out and unsure it pays off, more Gen Z students are getting in and not showing up—so colleges are cutting prices
items.summary:
For decades, getting into college meant convincing admissions officers you deserved a spot. Now some universities are doing the convincing: admitting students who haven’t applied, waiving application fees, and enlisting professors to personally recruit prospective freshmen, according to The Hechinger Report in a story also published by NPR .

The shift comes as colleges prepare for a shrinking pool of traditional college-age students while more young people reconsider the four-year path. For the schools that depend on tuition, an empty seat is revenue that never arrives.

An October report from Hanover Research , based on a July survey of 1,000 U.S. high school students ages 16 to 19, found that only 66% were interested in pursuing a bachelor’s degree, down from 79% in 2025. Interest in associate degrees rose from 36% to 45%.

The longer-term trend points the same way. The share of high school graduates going directly to college fell from 70% in 2016 to 63% in 2024, the most recent year available, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics .

That doesn’t mean enrollment is falling everywhere. Undergraduate enrollment rose 0.6% this fall, according to preliminary National Student Clearinghouse data . But with the number of U.S. high school graduates projected to fall from a record 3.9 million in 2025 to about 3.4 million a year by 2041 , according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education , many colleges face growing competition for each incoming class.

Even students who commit don’t always show up 

Attracting enough Gen Z applicants is only part of the…
items.t: Priced out and unsure it pays off, more Gen Z students are getting in and not showing up—so colleges are cutting prices

items.title: ‘I might live forever’: Inside billionaire Larry Connor’s no-email, 5-minute-block longevity routine
items.summary:
Billionaire Larry Connor’s pursuit of longevity has a sort of corporate brutality: optimize inputs, measure outputs, and delegate the rest.

The 76-year-old real-estate mogul makes every second count, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal . He doesn’t touch an email inbox. Associates screen his messages, print them out, and respond on his behalf, the Journal reports.

His days are carved into blocks as short as five minutes, punctuated by squash matches, yoga, and high-intensity interval sessions.

Connor is part of a growing cohort of ultra-wealthy Americans pouring tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars a year into concierge doctors, biohacking retreats, and AI-driven wellness routines in pursuit of a longer, sharper life .

Investors with more than $10 million in assets spend roughly four times as much on healthcare annually as less-wealthy peers, according to a 2018 UBS survey of wealthy investors , and more than half of those polled expected to reach 100.

Billionaires are planning for the long haul, too. In UBS’s 2025 Billionaire Ambitions report , 44% said they expect to live significantly longer than they did a decade ago, and many are making longer-term investments and revisiting their wills as a result.

Inside Connor’s 15-person health team 

Connor built his wealth through the Connor Group, the Ohio-based apartment investment firm he founded in 1992 with $400,000 and three properties. Today it manages about $5 billion in assets across 17 U.S. markets, according to the Connor Group .

According to the Journal , roughly 15 specialists—strength…

items.title: ‘A complete reversal’: China once feared becoming roadkill for Western automakers, but a quarter-century after joining the WTO, the tables have turned
items.summary:
There was a time when China worried about competing with European carmakers. In the years leading up to China joining the World Trade Organization in 2001, the warning that circulated in the auto industry was lang lai le : “ the wolf is coming .” 

The wolf was technically already inside the gates—China had worked with foreign carmakers like General Motors and Volkswagen in joint ventures since the 1980s—but joining the WTO meant giving up 100% tariffs and import quotas that shielded China’s domestic car industry from competitors abroad. 

But despite having to lower its trade barriers, China is now the dominant carmaker, producing over 7 million cars in the first quarter of 2026, according to the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers. That’s almost twice the production of every EU country and the U.K. combined (3.7 million) and more than the 2.6 million made in the U.S. 

EVs helped put China on top, to the point where the EU and U.S. imposed tariffs on Chinese-made models because Chinese government backing of the EV industry led to surplus production that’s flooding overseas markets with cheap exports. Meanwhile, weak domestic demand has forced Chinese carmakers to rely on sales abroad. 

Germany, whose vaunted auto industry faces an existential threat, may mandate joint ventures with China, just like China did with Volkswagen decades earlier to protect its automakers. 

“There’s been a complete reversal,” Eric Thun , professor of Chinese business studies at Oxford, told Fortune . 

How China did it 

As Beijing and local governments scrambled to meet…
items.t: ‘A complete reversal’: China once feared becoming roadkill for Western automakers, but a quarter-century after joining the WTO, the tables have turned

items.title: After Florida voted to slash property taxes, towns looking to fill budget holes may end up relying on the state: ‘The bailout comes with a leash’
items.summary:
Just about two weeks after Florida voters approved sweeping property tax cuts in the midterm election, officials in one Florida city are already planning for how they’ll make up for the lost revenue, including through a potential new fee on property owners to help pay for firefighters.

Florida’s Amendment 3 increases the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, which means the property tax bill for eligible homeowners will go down. Florida TaxWatch estimated that the measure could reduce local government revenue by $4.9 billion in its first fiscal year, and by $45.8 billion over five years.

Sanford, a city northeast of Orlando, expects to lose approximately $15 million in property tax revenue over the next two years, amounting to an estimated 18% hole in its budget, local news station FOX 35 Orlando reported .

As such, the city is considering major changes. Last Monday, Sanford commissioners discussed eliminating travel to meetings with the Florida League of Cities, cutting public arts spending, and even offering early retirement incentives similar to those used during the Great Recession, the news station reported.

The adjustments made in Sanford in anticipation of a budget shortfall come as Americans expressed widespread frustration over the cost of living in a midterm election that helped Democrats regain both chambers of Congress. 

Florida wasn’t the only state where voters passed property tax measures. In North Carolina, voters approved a constitutional amendment requiring lawmakers to limit increases in property…
items.t: After Florida voted to slash property taxes, towns looking to fill budget holes may end up relying on the state: ‘The bailout comes with a leash’

items.title: What a Tiny Chorus of the ‘Bring Back Jensen’ Tech Bros Gets Wrong
items.summary:
A small band of rogue tech bros has ridden to Jensen Huang’s defense amidst a report from the Financial Times that Huang is huddling with allies, plotting a comeback as Nvidia CEO days after resigning, with a petition demanding “due process, not mob justice,” signed by a minority of tech voices who have gotten outsized attention, such as Elon Musk and Atreides Management managing partner Gavin Baker. One tech bro even said , “Nvidia would be wrong to fire Jensen. His marital indiscretions are between him, his wife, and a reprimand from the board,” as if that was all there is to the story. 

But this small circle of rogue tech bros is wrong. This is not a story about a woke inquisition or prudes regulating marital indiscretions and sex – and a Sam Altman-style comeback does not make sense. We were supportive of Altman’s comeback and knew Steve Jobs personally – and supported his firing and subsequent comeback . But these circumstances are materially different.  There is no comeback here. 

Start with the conduct the defenders wave away, of Huang’s workplace affairs with direct subordinates. Huang admitted infidelity on Nov. 8. Days later, the New York Times reported a relationship with one of his direct reports. Nvidia’s code of conduct , which opens with a letter from Huang himself, names “personal relationships” as a conflict of interest. We had firsthand knowledge of Mark Hurd’s removal at HP over expense reports that concealed a personal relationship with a contractor, which was the right removal. Boards at McDonald’s, Intel and Nestlé similarly removed CEOs over…
items.t: What a Tiny Chorus of the ‘Bring Back Jensen’ Tech Bros Gets Wrong

items.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
items.summary:
Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks

The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.

Two years ago, residents of Oakland, California, woke up to a shocking scene: their mayor’s home was being raided by the FBI. Agents were seen carrying dozens of boxes from the hilltop home of Sheng Thao, the city’s 38-year-old leader, as part of an investigation constituents would later learn alleged her participation in a pay-to-play scheme with the city’s recycling contractor.

It was a stunning moment for Thao, who was elected to lead the Bay Area city in 2022 and was once seen as a promising young mayor in a city that has long grappled with economic inequality and a reputation for violent crime. Her story of growing up in a refugee family and overcoming domestic violence and homelessness to become the first person of Hmong descent to run a major US city resonated with readers confronting questions about equity and representation that came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, and made her the subject of glowing media profiles.

Gymshark, the £1bn British sportswear firm started in a family garage, is locked in a trademark battle that threatens the future of a small fitness business.

Ben Francis, the university dropout who started sewing his own gym clothes in his parents’ garage and is now estimated to be worth £800m, is trying to add The Conditioning Club to his Gymshark stable of trademarks.

items.title: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
items.summary:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings

World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.

items.t: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits

items.title: Italy fines Meta $887m for accessing Android users’ photos and videos
items.summary:
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech giant and Meta says it plans to appeal the decision

Italy’s data protection agency has fined Facebook parent company Meta €805m ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their specific consent.

Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users “without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them”, the authority said in a statement.

Continue reading...
items.t: Italy fines Meta $887m for accessing Android users’ photos and videos

items.title: A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and households are expected to pick up the tab
items.summary:
Raising borrowing costs too far risks laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy

A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.

Continue reading...
items.t: A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and households are expected to pick up the tab

items.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says
items.summary:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% this month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.

Continue reading...
items.t: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says

items.title: The weaknesses that cost Binance $6.3 billion are already hitting Europe’s banks
items.summary:
When hackers drained $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, on October 29, it was tempting to treat it as a crypto problem. Less than a week later, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a French lender, disclosed that hackers had made off with roughly €100 million ($112 million). 

The back-to-back attacks highlight the threat of cyber heists to traditional banks. “If a company like Binance can lose billions of dollars, the threats facing banks are overwhelming,” said Ryan Kirkley, cofounder and CEO of Global Settlement, which develops blockchain infrastructure for banks. Speaking at the Digital Asset Summit in London on November 10, he said: “It is impossible for the average bank to stay secure.” 

Binance’s founder and former CEO, Changpeng Zhao, went further. “If a crypto exchange can be hacked, banks are in a worse position, in my opinion,” he told CoinDesk days after the heist. 

The Binance hackers used a combination of social engineering and malicious software to take over crypto wallets and drain them of funds. This involved arranging a series of fake job interviews to persuade a Binance engineer to inadvertently download malware which allowed the hackers into the company’s systems. 

The FBI has seized $1.2 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency, while Binance confirmed it had “replenished” approximately 98% of the total impacted amount. 

The weaknesses hackers exploited to steal funds on Binance are not unique to crypto and the same vulnerabilities are present in traditional financial institutions, said Katerina Mitrokotsa, professor of…
items.t: The weaknesses that cost Binance $6.3 billion are already hitting Europe’s banks
